grand_strategy.reading: Mexico is a state that cooperates with its strongest neighbour in order to keep that neighbour out of its territory, and Sheinbaum, in office since October 2024, has held that line with a steady sovereignty language. Its posture toward the United States is reluctant partnership: it hands over cartel figures, accepts CIA flights and the National Guard at the border, and refuses troops and unilateral strikes, while the USMCA stays unrenewed and the tariff exemption is the lever of the 2026 review. Mexico hedges through the EU agreement and tariffs on Chinese goods rather than through alignment with anyone, so its foreign policy is measured less by the partners it picks than by how far Washington lets it pick. Its weakest flanks are at home: a judicial reform that frightens investors, a Pemex still losing money on about USD 80bn of debt, and a remittance flow that deportations and the 1% tax are already shrinking.

stances.note: Read from Mexico City, the mirror of the USA card, where Washington holds Mexico as partner with bond none. Mexico cooperates out of necessity and resists alignment: cartel figures handed over (Feb 2025, Jan 2026), CIA flights and the National Guard at the border accepted, but Sheinbaum rejects US troops (May 2025) and any US military action on Mexican soil ("no invasion", Aug 2025), and calls the CIA operations of May 2026 a breach she does not accept. The grade is structural: the tariffs of 4 Mar 2025 and the USMCA left unrenewed (1 Jul 2026) are not rupture, and Mexico is not rival because it does not seek Washington's defeat. Trend cooling: the new cartel designations (July 2026) and the rejection of the US claim that the Mexican government is linked to cartels (July 2026). Bond grievance, not none: the 1914 occupation of Veracruz (index pointer, the Tampico incident) is the historical wound, and Pew (2026, via Wikipedia) finds 55% of Mexicans with a negative view of the US. Tier-4 pointer for the bond; the grade rests on tier-3 reporting.
